title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Pain Assessment, Functional Goals & Reassessment
html:
Pain is a personal sensory and emotional experience. The client’s self-report is the primary source when the client can communicate reliably; vital signs, diagnosis, age, culture, behavior, or appearance do not prove or disprove it. A complete nursing assessment identifies the pain pattern, effect on function, safety risks, and response to the plan.

Learning goals

  • Complete a multidimensional pain assessment using PQRSTU or an equivalent structure.
  • Distinguish common nociceptive and neuropathic features without independently diagnosing the cause.
  • Select a valid pain tool for the client’s age, condition, and communication ability.
  • Assess pain in clients who cannot self-report.
  • Set an individualized comfort-function goal.
  • Reassess benefit, function, adverse effects, and need for escalation.

Screening is not a complete assessment

Asking whether pain is present or requesting one intensity number may screen for a problem. When pain is present, gather location, quality, onset, pattern, duration, radiation, severity, aggravating and relieving factors, associated symptoms, previous episodes and treatments, current therapies, beliefs and goals, and effects on sleep, mood, mobility, breathing, appetite, work, relationships, and daily activities.

Do not normalize a dangerous pain pattern
New chest pressure, sudden severe headache, pain with neurologic change, a painful pulseless or cool limb, severe pain out of proportion to findings, or rapidly worsening pain can signal an emergency. Stabilize and escalate according to the clinical situation rather than completing a routine questionnaire first.

Use PQRSTU to organize the story

  • P—Provocation/Palliation: What brings it on or makes it better or worse?
  • Q—Quality/Quantity: What does it feel like? How much does it interfere?
  • R—Region/Radiation: Where is it, and does it travel?
  • S—Severity: What rating or descriptor fits now, at best, and at worst?
  • T—Timing/Treatment: When did it start, is it constant or intermittent, and what has been tried?
  • U—Understanding/You: What does the client think is happening, and what matters most?

PQRSTU is a prompt, not a script. Clarify inconsistencies respectfully. A client who calls pain “tolerable” while rating it 7/10 may mean it is 7 with movement but manageable at rest. Context changes the plan.

Recognize features that guide assessment

Nociceptive pain arises from actual or threatened tissue injury. Somatic pain may be localized and described as aching, throbbing, or sharp; visceral pain may be diffuse, cramping, pressure-like, or referred. Neuropathic pain is related to lesion or disease of the somatosensory system and may be burning, electric, shooting, tingling, or accompanied by altered sensation. Mixed patterns occur. Descriptors inform focused assessment and communication but do not allow the RN to assign a medical diagnosis without the required evaluation.

Acute pain often accompanies recent injury, illness, or procedure; chronic pain persists beyond expected healing or accompanies a long-term condition. Chronic pain may occur without tachycardia, grimacing, or other obvious behavior. Never use normal vital signs as proof that the client is not in pain.

Choose the scale for the client

Use a consistent, validated tool appropriate to age, developmental level, language, cognition, sensory ability, and clinical setting. A numeric rating scale is useful only if the client understands it. A verbal descriptor or validated faces scale may fit another client. Explain the anchors and let the client choose the score; the RN does not select a face based on how distressed the client looks.

Use the same tool for reassessment when possible so the trend is meaningful. A score from one scale is not automatically equivalent to the same number on another. Record the tool, conditions such as rest or movement, location, and relevant functional task.

When the client cannot self-report

First optimize communication: glasses, hearing aids, simple questions, communication boards, interpreters, yes/no signals, or other aids. If reliable self-report remains impossible, use a validated behavioral pain tool designed for the population and setting. Assess facial expression, body movement, muscle tension, vocalization, consolability, activity, and ventilator interaction as the selected tool requires.

Review likely painful conditions and procedures, ask caregivers about baseline behavior, and observe response to comfort measures. Behavior scores suggest the presence and change of pain-related behavior; they do not translate directly into the client’s self-reported intensity. Absence of behavior—especially with sedation, paralysis, or severe neurologic impairment—does not prove absence of pain.

Assess beliefs, risk, and prior response

Ask what pain means to the client, which strategies have helped, and whether concerns about adverse effects, dependence, cost, or cultural expectations affect reporting. Review medications, allergies, kidney or liver considerations, respiratory and neurologic status, sleep-disordered breathing, falls, substance-use history, and other client-specific risks according to the care plan. Avoid stigma: a history of substance use does not eliminate the right to pain assessment and safe treatment.

Set a comfort-function goal

Collaborate on a realistic outcome tied to what the client needs to do, such as deep breathe, sleep, transfer, walk, eat, or participate in therapy. The goal is not automatically zero pain. “Pain no higher than 3/10 at rest and able to cough and walk to the chair” is more informative than an isolated number. Goals and acceptable tradeoffs should reflect the client’s priorities and safety.

Match the plan and monitor risk

Use ordered pharmacologic and appropriate nonpharmacologic strategies as part of an individualized multimodal plan. Positioning, splinting, heat or cold when safe, relaxation, breathing, reduced stimulation, activity pacing, mobility, sleep support, and other methods may help depending on the cause and client preference. Check contraindications and protect skin and sensation.

Before medications, review the order, last dose, allergies, pain and function, sedation and respiratory status, relevant vital signs and laboratory data, interactions, route, and risk factors. After treatment, assess both desired and unintended effects. New excessive sedation, slowed or difficult breathing, hypotension, confusion, weakness, fall risk, nausea, constipation, urinary retention, or other deterioration requires prompt response.

Reassessment closes the loop

Reassess at the time appropriate to the route, intervention, condition, and policy. Use the same scale and comparable conditions when possible. Evaluate intensity, function, comfort goal, adverse effects, and the client’s judgment of benefit. If the plan is ineffective or harm is emerging, do not simply repeat the intervention; assess the cause, protect the client, communicate, and revise the plan through the appropriate process.

Document what can guide the next decision

Record location, quality, intensity and scale, timing, associated findings, function, comfort goal, intervention, reassessment time, response, adverse effects, communication, and plan changes. “Pain better” is less useful than “45 minutes after ordered oral analgesic, pain decreased from 7/10 to 4/10; client coughed and walked 20 feet; alert with unchanged respirations; goal partly met.”

Clinical example

A client one day after surgery reports pain 7/10 but lies quietly. The RN accepts the report, learns that pain occurs mainly with coughing and prevents deep breathing, assesses sedation and respiratory status, reviews the plan and last dose, and collaborates on a goal of tolerable pain while coughing and walking. After ordered and nonpharmacologic measures, the RN reassesses pain, respiratory status, alertness, and the client’s ability to cough and mobilize.
